strengths: Extensive and well-designed empirical study: results are reported on two major benchmarks (SUPERB, HEAR) plus downstream fine-tuning (ASR, AudioSet tagging), across three model scales (94M/327M/600M) and both single- and dual-domain settings, giving a fairly complete picture of the method's behavior.

The core idea—using multi-codebook vector quantization (MVQ) of teacher SSL representations to produce fine-grained discrete targets for masked prediction—is a sensible and, to my knowledge, novel bridge between the token-prediction paradigm popular in speech SSL and the more irregular acoustic structure of general audio, addressing a genuine gap (domain-specific SSL objectives).

Strong quantitative results: the speech-only SPEAR model matches or beats WavLM Large on 12/15 SUPERB tasks under matched data/model size, and the dual-domain model narrows the gap to single-domain specialists while outperforming a similarly-scoped concurrent unified model (USAD) on both SUPERB and HEAR.

Thorough ablation studies (Appendix G) examining teacher choice, α weighting of masked/unmasked loss, number of codebooks, dual-domain loss balancing strategies, and a qualitative UMAP analysis showing MVQ preserves speaker identity far better than k-means — these add genuine mechanistic insight beyond simple benchmark numbers.

Honest reporting of limitations and negative results (e.g., VC degradation with scale, weaker HEAR scores vs. much larger Dasheng 1.2B, imbalanced data mixture hurting audio-side unification), which strengthens the credibility of the empirical claims.
weaknesses: The method is essentially knowledge distillation from strong existing domain-specific teacher models (WavLM Large, Dasheng 1.2B) reframed as an 'SSL' objective; the student's ceiling is shown in the teacher-selection ablation (G.1) to be closely tied to teacher quality, which somewhat undercuts the framing of SPEAR as an independent, generalizable SSL recipe rather than a compression/distillation pipeline contingent on pre-existing strong single-domain models.

The core technical novelty is limited: MVQ itself is taken directly from prior work (Guo et al., 2023), and the masked-token-prediction objective is a well-established SSL recipe (HuBERT-style); the contribution is mainly the combination and application to a dual-domain setting rather than a fundamentally new method.

Evidence for genuine 'unification' is mixed: the dual-domain model shows slight degradations on several SUPERB understanding/paralinguistic tasks relative to the speech-only variant, and on HEAR the unified XLarge model trails the (much larger, more data-rich) Dasheng 1.2B on environment and music tasks; the claimed synergy is real but modest and partly obscured by an acknowledged imbalanced data mixture (87% speech).

No code or checkpoints are available at submission time (deferred to post-review), which limits independent verification of the many benchmark numbers despite otherwise good documentation of hyperparameters.

Some comparisons across tables mix different pre-training data scales and model sizes (e.g., Dasheng-Base with 20x more data, WavLM Large vs. differently-sized SPEAR variants), which, while transparently disclosed, makes some 'state-of-the-art' claims less clean and requires careful reading to properly contextualize.

strengths: Extremely extensive empirical evaluation across two major benchmarks (SUPERB, HEAR) plus LibriSpeech ASR and AudioSet tagging fine-tuning, with multiple model scales (94M/327M/600M), giving a broad picture of the method's behavior.

The core empirical result that fine-grained MVQ tokens as masked-prediction targets outperform coarse k-means/random-projection tokens is well supported, e.g. the speech model beats WavLM Large on most SUPERB tasks with matched data/size, and student models consistently outperform their own teacher models across several ablations (Table 16, 17), which is a genuinely useful and somewhat surprising finding.

Thorough ablation studies (teacher choice, alpha weighting, codebook count, dual-domain loss balancing, UMAP visualization of feature subspaces) that go beyond the typical superficial ablation and provide some mechanistic insight into why the method works.
Reasonably clear writing and explicit reproducibility/ethics statements, with a promise to release code and checkpoints.
weaknesses: The framing as a novel 'SSL framework' is questionable: the method is fundamentally a knowledge-distillation scheme that requires two already-trained, large domain-specific SSL teachers (WavLM Large, Dasheng 1.2B) to generate targets via MVQ. Ablations (Appendix G.1) explicitly show performance is teacher-bounded (weaker HuBERT teacher yields a weaker student), meaning SPEAR does not obviate the need for prior domain-specific pretraining -- it repackages it. This undercuts the central motivating claim that the paper solves the 'domain-specific tailoring' problem described in the introduction.

The 'unification' achieved by the dual-domain model is not a strong emergent property but an engineered outcome of an asymmetric loss requiring two separate frozen teachers simultaneously; the resulting unified model shows measurable degradation relative to single-domain specialists on several SUPERB and HEAR sub-tasks (e.g., understanding/paralinguistic tasks, VC task where larger unified models underperform the Base model), so the practical benefit of 'one model that does both' vs. simply using two specialist models is not conclusively established.

Audio-side performance remains a clear weak point: the audio teacher (Dasheng 1.2B) was trained on 272k hours vs. only 13k hours available for SPEAR's own audio-domain pretraining, and consequently SPEAR's audio/dual-domain models still trail Dasheng 1.2B substantially on speech- and music-related HEAR sub-tasks, an issue the authors themselves acknowledge but leave unresolved ("we leave this as an important direction for future work").

Novelty is somewhat incremental: MVQ itself is taken directly from Guo et al. (2023) (originally proposed for representation compression/KD), and the backbone architecture (Zipformer with multi-resolution encoding) is adopted wholesale from Yao et al. (2024). The paper's contribution is largely the combination/application of these existing components to a masked-prediction pretext task rather than a new algorithmic idea.

Many reported improvements are small in absolute magnitude (e.g., 0.1 WER, sub-1-point mAP/HEAR differences) and no error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported anywhere in the main paper or appendix, making it hard to assess whether claimed 'state-of-the-art' or '12/15 tasks' improvements are robust rather than noise.

The comparison basis for 'first unified SSL framework' is not fully convincing given closely related concurrent/prior work (USAD, MT2KD, Gong et al. 2022) that pursue very similar goals; the paper distinguishes itself mainly on the choice of SSL objective vs. feature-matching KD, but this distinction, while empirically favorable in the reported comparison, is not deeply analyzed for why it should generalize.

No computational/efficiency analysis is provided despite the pipeline requiring pre-training and running two frozen teacher models plus separate MVQ quantiser training for every domain, which is a nontrivial practical overhead compared to standard single-teacher SSL pretraining that is not discussed.

strengths: Proposes a genuinely novel and well-motivated unification of speech and audio SSL via fine-grained multi-codebook vector quantisation (MVQ) tokens, addressing a real limitation of coarse k-means-based token prediction in the audio domain.

Very extensive empirical validation across two major benchmarks (SUPERB and HEAR) plus downstream fine-tuning on ASR and audio tagging, at three model scales (Base/Large/XLarge up to 600M params), providing strong evidence for the claims.
Speech-domain model matches or exceeds the strong WavLM Large baseline on 12/15 SUPERB tasks under a matched-data, matched-size comparison, which is a rigorous and convincing head-to-head result.

Thorough and informative ablation studies (Appendix G) covering teacher model choice, masked/unmasked loss weighting, number of codebooks, dual-domain training strategy, and a qualitative UMAP analysis showing MVQ tokens retain speaker information that k-means discards — these ablations meaningfully deepen understanding of why the method works.
The asymmetrical dual-domain loss design is empirically justified via a 3-way comparison (JOINT/DISJOINT/ASYMMETRICAL), showing it is not an arbitrary design choice.
Good transparency about limitations (e.g., VC underperformance, imbalanced audio data causing HEAR gaps vs Dasheng 1.2B) rather than hiding weak results.
Reproducibility statement with commitment to release code and checkpoints, plus detailed hyperparameter tables in the appendix.
weaknesses: The framework fundamentally relies on strong pre-existing teacher models (WavLM Large, Dasheng 1.2B) to generate MVQ targets, making the approach closer to a distillation-plus-SSL-objective hybrid; while the paper argues the students can surpass their teachers on individual metrics, overall representation quality (e.g., on HEAR speech/music categories) still lags behind the larger, more heavily-trained Dasheng 1.2B teacher, suggesting the framework's ceiling is still influenced by teacher/data quality.

General audio pre-training data (13k hours) is substantially smaller and less diverse than speech data (84k-197k hours), leading to a persistent imbalance that shows up as degraded performance on some audio/music tasks for the dual-domain models relative to single-domain audio models — a limitation the authors acknowledge but do not resolve.

The 'first unified SSL framework' framing is somewhat strong given related prior work (Gong et al. 2022, USAD/Chang et al. 2025) already explores joint speech+audio pretraining; while the paper differentiates its objective (mask-token-prediction SSL loss vs. feature-matching KD), the novelty framing could be tempered.

Results on some SUPERB tasks (ST, QbE, VC) and the VC generation task specifically show the dual/single-domain SPEAR models underperforming baselines or degrading with scale, which is not fully explained beyond a brief hypothesis about overfitting.

The additional training complexity and computational overhead of training separate MVQ quantisers per teacher domain, plus maintaining two frozen large teacher models during pre-training, is not discussed in terms of resource cost, which is relevant for reproducibility/practical adoption.

The λ hyperparameter (weighting the audio-specific loss in dual-domain training) appears fixed at 0.1 without an ablation showing sensitivity, despite this being a potentially important balance parameter.

strengths: Extensive empirical validation across two major benchmarks (SUPERB, HEAR) plus fine-tuning on ASR and audio tagging, with results consistently outperforming or matching strong baselines (WavLM Large, USAD, BEATs, EAT, ATST-Frame) across multiple model scales (Base/Large/XLarge).

Thorough and well-designed ablation studies covering teacher model choice, teacher layer selection, number of MVQ codebooks, masked/unmasked loss weighting (alpha), encoder architecture (Zipformer vs Transformer), and MVQ vs k-means targets, giving good insight into which design choices matter and why.

A controlled, fair comparison against the closest competitor USAD (matching teacher models and comparable data scale) convincingly demonstrates that SPEAR's masked-token-prediction + KD combination outperforms USAD's pure feature-matching approach, supporting the paper's core methodological claim.

The asymmetrical dual-domain loss and token mixing mechanism are both independently motivated and ablated against sensible alternatives (JOINT/DISJOINT strategies; WavLM-style denoising vs no augmentation), with results supporting the design choices, particularly clear gains on speaker diarization/separation/enhancement from token mixing.

The paper shows the student can outperform its own teacher (e.g., SPEARs Large > WavLM Large; audio Base models > ATST-frame teacher), which is a meaningful and non-trivial validation that the framework is not simply upper-bounded by teacher quality.

Reasonably transparent about limitations of the dual-domain model relative to single-domain specialists and relative to much larger-data models like Dasheng 1.2B, and provides an interpretability analysis (UMAP of MVQ codebook subspaces) that adds some mechanistic insight into why MVQ tokens help.
Good coverage of architectural and training details in the appendix to support reproducibility (hyperparameters, GPU hours, model configs), with a promise to release code/pretrained models.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: MVQ (Guo et al. 2023), masked token prediction (HuBERT-style), and knowledge distillation from domain teachers are all pre-existing techniques; the main contribution is their combination plus two secondary tricks (asymmetric loss, token mixing), which is a reasonable but modest advance rather than a fundamentally new idea.

The audio-domain performance of SPEAR still meaningfully trails much larger-data specialized models (e.g., Dasheng 1.2B on HEAR), and the dual-domain unified model shows performance degradation relative to single-domain specialists on several understanding/paralinguistic and HEAR music/environment tasks, somewhat undercutting the 'unified representation' narrative even as the paper is honest about this.

SUPERB tasks such as ST, QbE, and VC show no improvement (or are not improved) over WavLM Large, which is glossed over briefly without deeper analysis of why the method may not transfer to these tasks.

Music-domain pre-training data is quite limited (only ~4.8k hours across two datasets) relative to speech and general-audio data, which likely explains weaker music results but is not thoroughly explored as a controlled variable (e.g., no ablation isolating the effect of increasing music-specific data).

The framework's ceiling is inherently dependent on the availability and quality of strong pre-existing domain-specific teachers; while ablations show the framework benefits from stronger teachers, this dependency somewhat limits the claimed self-sufficiency of the 'self-supervised' framing, since the fine-grained MVQ targets are themselves derived from other SSL models' representations rather than the raw signal.
Code and pretrained models are only promised for release, not yet available, so full reproducibility cannot be currently verified despite fairly detailed hyperparameter/appendix documentation.

The paper does not provide a systematic compute/efficiency comparison against baselines in the main text (e.g., total training compute vs. USAD, Dasheng), which would help contextualize whether reported gains come partly from more efficient use of similar compute or simply from more compute/data.
